title: Best Sleeping Bags UK
short: Down and synthetic sleeping bags compared by warmth-to-weight ratio, packed size and weather resistance, from budget picks to ultralight premium bags.
intro: A sleeping bag's warmth-to-weight ratio and temperature rating matter more than price alone, and down versus synthetic fill changes how it performs in damp UK conditions. This guide compares bags tested by Live for the Outdoors' team on real nights out in the hills, assessed in the conditions each bag is designed for.

products.name: Xenith III
products.best_for: Spring-to-autumn UK hill and mountain use
products.summary: LFTO's top three-season pick, the lightest bag tested at just 690g with a very good warmth-to-weight ratio from luxury 900-fill down and a superlight 10D shell. Vertical chest baffles and slanted body baffles maximise heat retention, with a full-length zip and integrated draught collar, though it comes at a high price.
products.search: Mountain Equipment Xenith III sleeping bag

products.name: Orbit 0°
products.best_for: Budget-conscious campers who don't need to carry the bag far
products.key_spec: 1,450g, Hollowfibre synthetic insulation, recycled shell fabric
products.summary: LFTO found this comfortable, warm, durable and sustainable, with Hollowfibre synthetic insulation that beats down bags on price and stays effective even in damp conditions. It's genuinely bulky and heavy compared to rivals, but a draft collar, adjustable hood and zip-coupling compatibility round out a strong package.

products.name: Ultra 0°
products.best_for: Backpackers who want minimum pack weight without sacrificing warmth
products.key_spec: 600g, 850-fill goose down, comfort to around 2°C, 5 sizes available
products.summary: LFTO was impressed that just 295g of high-loft 850-fill down gives this bag a genuinely warm rating at only 600g total weight. It's available in five sizes (rare for a sleeping bag) and is highly sustainable with recycled Pertex Quantum fabric, though the ultralight 10D shell is delicate and needs careful handling.

products.name: Neutrino 400
products.best_for: Buyers who want a fully-featured, tried-and-tested design
products.key_spec: Adjustable hood, 3/4-length YKK zip, chevron baffle design
products.summary: A standout from Rab's versatile Neutrino range, hand-stuffed and fully featured, that LFTO says has earned multiple top awards over the years. A unique chevron-style baffle arrangement (rather than horizontal) gives more loft and fewer cold spots using less material, plus newly implemented PFC-free and recycled-material sustainability upgrades.
cons: Narrow mummy shape won't suit everyone

products.name: Soul 15/25
products.best_for: Campers who prioritise comfort and ventilation over minimum weight
products.key_spec: 1.2kg, synthetic fill, innovative draft guard, dual-sided ventilation
products.summary: A synthetic bag LFTO found especially suited to wet environments, with a water-resistant material that copes fine with accidental condensation contact inside the tent. An innovative draft guard extends over the face and tightens with a drawcord, while vents on both the zip and foot allow genuinely excellent ventilation control.
pros: Fully recyclable at end of life
cons: Warmth-to-weight ratio not as good as down

products.name: Leviathan EV 900 Down
products.best_for: Budget winter campers who don't need premium fill power
products.summary: LFTO calls the price one of the biggest positives, offering a -9°C comfort rating and hydrophobic down treatment at a genuinely low cost, good for camping just below zero. A decent neck collar baffle and hood help, though build quality and insulation feel less premium than pricier winter bags on this list.

products.name: Fly Creek UL25
products.best_for: Ultralight backpackers who prioritise minimum weight above all else
products.summary: A premium ultralight bag LFTO found offers impressive warmth for its weight, packing down to just 24 x 20cm while rated to +2°C comfort. High-quality 850-fill down and diamond quilting deliver genuine performance, made from recycled fishing net fabric, though the slim tapered fit may feel restrictive for broader builds and the half-length zip limits ventilation.
cons: Half zip can snag and limits ventilation
Tapered fit isn't ideal for broad frames
products.search: Big Agnes Fly Creek UL25 sleeping bag

products.name: Trestles Elite Eco 30
products.best_for: Buyers who want synthetic reliability with genuine sustainability credentials
products.key_spec: Fully recycled materials, HL-ElixR Eco insulation, full-length snag-resistant zip
products.summary: LFTO has consistently been impressed by this bag's combination of high performance and sustainable materials, built entirely from recycled fabric including innovative HL-ElixR Eco insulation. It offers a very good warmth-to-weight ratio for a synthetic bag and maintains insulation even when damp, in a relatively compact pack size for the category.
pros: Very good warmth-to-weight ratio for synthetic fill
cons: Still heavier than equivalent down bags
products.search: Marmot Trestles Elite Eco 30 sleeping bag

guide.a: Down, like the Mountain Equipment Xenith III or Exped Ultra 0° here, gives the best warmth-to-weight ratio and packs smaller, but loses much of its insulating power when wet unless treated with a hydrophobic coating. Synthetic fill, like the Nemo Soul or Marmot Trestles Elite Eco here, is heavier and bulkier but keeps insulating even when damp, which suits genuinely wet UK conditions.

guide.q: What do comfort and limit temperature ratings mean?
guide.a: The comfort rating is the lowest temperature at which an average person should sleep comfortably, while the limit rating is the lowest temperature at which they can sleep without waking from cold, though not necessarily comfortably. It's generally safer to buy for the comfort rating of the coldest conditions you expect, not the limit rating.

guide.q: How much does fill power matter?
guide.a: Fill power measures how much a given weight of down expands to trap air, so a higher number (like the Exped's 850 or Mountain Equipment's 900) means more warmth for less weight and bulk. Lower fill power bags, like the OEX's 600, can still perform well but need more down by weight to achieve the same warmth.

guide.q: Is an ultralight sleeping bag worth the extra cost?
guide.a: For backpacking where every gram in your pack matters, an ultralight bag like the Big Agnes or Exped here is a genuine, worthwhile investment. For car camping or shorter trips where you're not carrying the bag far, a heavier but cheaper option, like the Deuter Orbit here, gives most of the comfort without the premium price.
